extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, psychology, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and comparison of historical and psychological theories about what produces laughter and what counts as 'humor' (e.g., play-attitude, disappointment, mechanical overflow, benign humor). Extracts criteria and empirical observations about comic effects and joke durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-attitude as necessary condition for tickling laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The play-attitude (a pleasurable state of mind which welcomes fun) is a definite condition of the nervous systems for tickling laughter; tickling 'must fit in with a particular mood' and the dreadfully serious or preoccupied child will not respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance from Sully and Darwin: the child's mind must be in 'a pleasurable condition' for tickling to produce laughter; examples include a stranger nursing causing alarm that bars play, a cross or vaccinated child not giving genial response, or mental preoccupation preventing response. The page treats play as the instinctual attitude in which laughter mingles with defensive movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment Theory (strained expectation causing laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strained expectation which comes to absolutely nothing may cause a humorous recoil; laughter can follow when expectation for something significant is thwarted by something trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Aristotle and Kant and supported by experiments (Dumont, Lillien J. Martin, H. L. Hollingsworth). Examples: business-like tickling vs playful tickling; William Hazlitt's aphorism 'We weep at what thwarts ... we laugh at what only disappoints our expectations in trifles.' The theory explains why practical jokes can often be enjoyed only once (they rely on a 'strained expectation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness and contrast (novelty) as comic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An element of 'unexpectedness' and of 'contrast' is always present in things at which people laugh; novelty (strangeness) often triggers mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental support: Martin's subjects selected Schopenhauer's definition and reported unexpectedness/contrast. Cultural corroboration: Sanskrit treatises (Dasarupa, Sahitya Darpana) describe mirth as caused by 'strange' or 'distorted' actions, words, or attire. Observation: children and 'savages' greet anything new with laughter — novelty drives comic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapidity of repeated jokes / familiarity reduces comic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes, as they grow familiar and capable of being quickly anticipated, cease to have any comic quality; repeated exposure generally makes jokes wane in value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hollingsworth's experiments produced curves showing the rate at which various jokes wane; while all jokes wane more rapidly than other verbal objects of esteem, different jokes wane at different rates and completeness. Some jokes even gain slightly in value on subsequent acquaintance. Practical jokes tend to lose value fastest because they require a strained expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability differences by joke type (poetic vs practical; meaning vs absurdity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic jokes endure longer than practical jokes; jokes whose value lies mainly in what they mean endure longer than those whose main value is the absurdity of their seeming not to mean what they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hollingsworth's findings: certain groups of jokes appreciated at first lose value faster than others; poetic jokes (value in wording/meaning) are more durable, while practical/absurdity-based jokes ('not meaning what they seem') fade quickly. This nuance modifies a crude 'repetition kills all jokes' rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic from 'strangeness' or 'distortion' (Sanskrit dramatists)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic may arise from perceiving something 'strange' or 'distorted' in form, speech, or gesture — this 'substantial' element of the comic produces mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations from Dasarupa and Sahitya Darpana: mirth (hasa) caused by strange actions, words, attire; stage theory: comic excitants apprehended by sympathy/identification of spectator with actor are necessary to experience the comic flavor. Provides an objective description of comic objects on stage consistent with joke-based comic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign humor: absence of scorn and presence of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: True or 'benign' humor is characterized by an absence of scorn, a presence of emotion, and a genial, excellent quality — humor springs partly from the heart and issues in sympathy or still smiles rather than contemptuous laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary extracted from many definitions: 'absence of scorn', 'presence of emotion', and 'humor is an excellent thing.' Carlyle: 'True humor springs not more from the head than from the heart...it is not contempt, its essence is love.' Jean Paul and others present humor as promoting sympathy for mankind; this is contrasted with satirical or derisive laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest humor invites sympathetic identification (character enjoys superiority to circumstance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest form of comedy/humor invites a sympathetic experience in which the character himself enjoys his superiority to circumstance; humor can produce inward rejoicing without bitterness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hegel's formulation: 'Inseparable from the comic is an infinite geniality and confidence...experiencing therein no taint of bitterness.' Examples: Aristophanes, Falstaff; Sanskrit dramatists: spectators identify with actor and so experience the comic sentiment sympathetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Theory: laughter as overflow of nervous energy (Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is an overflow, along the most ready channels, of nervous energy stored up too full; it occurs when we prepare for something big and something small follows (descending incongruity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer's physiology: acrobat then clown example — energy prepared for spectacle is suddenly superfluous and 'floods forth' into muscles of voice/respiration/face. The page notes Spencer's eminence and that Lipps built a psychology atop this physiology; also includes critiques that this is too mechanical and cannot account for all comic situations (e.g., the 'aunt in the closet' example).

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic feeling is unique (Lipps): 'merriment' and feeling of smallness
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of the comic is a distinct feeling 'of the comic and nothing else'; its ground-color is a kind of merriment (Heiterkeit) — a feeling of smallness, lightness, and play that can be either pleasurable or painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lipps rejects reduction of the comic to other emotions and characterizes it psychologically: seriousness = feeling of greatness; merriment = feeling of smallness/the superficial/the light. He links these feelings to the relation of prepared psychic energy to the demand of an object of attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descending incongruity / 'something little' as the comic contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is a 'descending incongruity' where a relatively 'little' or 'meaningless' thing forms one side of the contrast, and crucially it is the second side — the goal of perception — that makes the contrast laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lipps' example: a tiny house next to great palaces is comic, whereas a row of palaces interrupted by a church arouses wonder not laughter. The 'little' must be the goal/endpoint of perception; the page explains why some quantitative contrasts produce wonder while others produce comic amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises when playful annoyances prevent serious adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh not at slight quantitative disappointments but when playful annoyances are extreme enough to rob us of the possibility of serious adjustment; comic laughter often follows when expectation and adjustment mechanisms fail in a playful context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: the clown meticulously dusting a horse's flank (too little) and then giving a resounding whack (too much) both provoke comic responses; acrobatic juggler argument and apples-throwing routine where performer catches apples in a comic way. This clarifies why not all disparities produce laughter — only those that disrupt normal adjustment in a playful way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor can enrich art by elevating the ugly (Weisse/Lotze)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor may enrich art by raising the ugly and distasteful into its domain — defining the comic as 'ugliness elevated' or 'the reconstitution of beauty out of her absolute negation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical defense against Hegel: Lotze and Weisse argue that the comic does not empty the world of Idea but rejoices that the Idea remains underlying; humor can thus confer objective aesthetic value, turning negative/ugly elements into part of art's domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a reflective ethical/spiritual stance (Lazarus: 'religion of the mind')
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be construed as a mental-religious attitude: the humorous mind recognizes its own imperfection (humiliation) yet is elevated and purified by consciousness of the Idea and the Infinite, producing a tempered, inwardly reconciled attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lazarus' statement: the two elements parallel religion — humble recognition of finitude and simultaneous elevation toward the Infinite. This criterion frames humor as an ethical/philosophical disposition rather than merely a comic mechanism.
